titleSource: Income Autopilot I: Finding the Muse

sittings.bodyEn: A muse is a small offer built to throw off cash while taking little of your week. The chapter sets three gates before you fall in love with an idea: a test that costs no more than five hundred dollars, a path to automation inside four weeks, and a running load of no more than one day a week. The aim is to own that vehicle. Hourly services fight the aim, because each new customer asks for more of you. Cash and time are the two currencies that make later projects possible. Treat every feature beyond those gates as optional.

terms.hook: A small automated offer that funds a defined life and keeps going with little of your week.

sittings.bodyEn: A shirt line can sell online and still die once wholesale and local discounting enter the picture. Each extra reseller tends to cut the advertised price, profit vanishes, and reorders stop, which is why a product can need a replacement every month. One supplement company did the opposite: it proved interest with a cheap book ad, then sold only through one national chain at a high price. Exclusivity can buy better margins, better in-store support, and faster payment. You may set a minimum advertised price even when you cannot set the final selling price. Choose the path to the customer before you commit to the product, and make sure every middleman still leaves you a profit.

terms.hook: A floor on what resellers may advertise, used to stop a race to the bottom.

sittings.bodyEn: Filling demand is easier than creating it, so start from a group you already belong to or understand. List those groups from your work, hobbies, and the publications you already read, then keep the ones with their own magazines. Call the advertising desk, ask for the rate card, the readership, and sample back issues, and notice which companies keep paying for ads that sell straight to those readers. The chapter's size screen is a full-page ad under five thousand dollars and at least fifteen thousand readers. The useful question is whether they spend, not whether they are rich. A small group you can actually reach beats a famous audience you cannot afford to address.

terms.hook: A specific group with its own media, small enough that your first ad budget can find them.

sittings.bodyEn: Brainstorm with two familiar markets that pass the magazine screen, and spend nothing while you brainstorm. The main benefit has to fit in one sentence a stranger can repeat. Price the sale between fifty and two hundred dollars, high enough that you need fewer customers and attract fewer complaints. Aim for a markup of about eight to ten times, so a hundred-dollar product costs you roughly ten to twelve dollars, with room for a late supplier. Manufacturing has to finish inside three to four weeks, and one to two weeks is the better target, which you confirm by asking contract makers for costs at several quantities. If the offer cannot be explained in a solid online help page, travel will collapse under questions.

terms.hook: The single claim a stranger can repeat, which is the signal to proceed.
A price about eight to ten times your cost, so a mistake does not erase the product.

sittings.bodyEn: Reselling an existing product is the fastest start and the least durable profit, unless an exclusive deal blocks other sellers. It works well as a later offer to people who already bought from you. Ask the maker for a wholesale list, often about forty percent off retail, form a simple company if a tax number is required, and do not buy stock until the next chapter's test. Licensing has two seats: the inventor can collect roughly three to ten percent of the wholesale price, and the licensee does the making and selling for the rest. That path is heavy on deals, so the chapter sends most readers toward creating. Confirm the margin and gather photos before any of these routes spend real money.

terms.hook: The inventor takes a small percent of wholesale, and the seller keeps the rest of the work and the profit.

sittings.bodyEn: Creation can be a prototype built from your description, or a stock item with your label on it. Gadgets often fail the test on tooling cost. Information is the class that clears the filters: small runs can be ready in under a week, and markups of twenty to fifty times are common. A physical hit is often copied within months, while a full course is slow to clone well. You can write the material, reuse public-domain sources after a lawyer checks them, or pay an expert a fee or a royalty around five to ten percent. Expert, in this chapter, means you know more than the buyer. A minimal customer base is the smallest number of those buyers needed to fund one named dream.

terms.hook: A how-to in audio, text, or video, fast to make and slow for rivals to copy well.
A stock item made for you and sold under your name.
The smallest number of buyers you must persuade to fund one specific dream.

sittings.bodyEn: Join two or three trade groups with names a stranger would recognize. Read three leading books on the topic and put each one onto a single summary page. Give one free seminar of one to three hours at a known university, then repeat it at two large local companies, and record the sessions. You may also offer a trade magazine one article, or an interview with a known expert if they decline your byline. Then answer requests from journalists so the groups, the talks, and the articles become public mentions. These are credibility indicators, which are what the market treats as proof. State only what you have done, in its best true light.

terms.hook: A group, a talk, a byline, or a media mention that the market reads as proof.

sittings.bodyEn: The chapter's three-day drill is one phone call a day to someone whose work you already follow. Call before eight thirty in the morning or after six at night, and send email only after the call fails. Bring one question you have researched and still cannot answer. Tell the gatekeeper you need two minutes, and ask them to help you through. At the end, ask whether a rare later question can travel by email. Aim at the top of the field. A smaller target makes the fear smaller and the practice weaker.

terms.hook: One researched question, requested by phone, with a door left open for later email.

sittings.bodyEn: Write the week you want and the monthly profit it requires, then pick two familiar markets that pass the magazine screen. For each, draft one sentence of benefit, a price inside the fifty to two hundred band, and a build time inside four weeks. Reject anything that needs you on the phone for every order. For an information offer, answer four prompts: a general skill narrowed to this market, a skill you would pay to learn, an expert you could record, and a failure you already climbed out of. Combine formats until the price feels fair, such as audio plus a short transcript and a quick-start guide, and digital delivery is allowed. Stop before you buy inventory, because the next chapter is the test.

A muse has to fund a life you already described and keep ordinary sales moving when you leave the daily work. The market can be small if you can name where those people gather and what an ad there costs. The offer needs one clear benefit, a price with room for ads and help, a short build, and an explanation that fits on a help page. Inventory and a live service you personally perform sit on the far side of that screen. Who may sell it, and how low they may advertise it, is chosen before you commit. Recall which offer survives the screen.
sittings.prompt: Which offer fits this chapter's muse?
choices: A narrow product you can reach through a real publication, priced with room for ads, that can keep selling after you leave the daily work
A custom service you deliver live for each buyer
A product you manufacture in bulk before anyone has paid
A huge audience you cannot name a magazine for
